title: Porridge with Peanut Butter
subtitle: Warming oat porridge stirred with peanut butter and topped with banana
excerpt: Peanut butter stirred into porridge just before serving melts into the oats and adds a nutty richness that keeps you going well into the morning. Banana on top and a drizzle of honey, and it is as good as breakfast gets on a cold weekday.
sourceNotes: Peanut butter porridge is a widely made modern British breakfast variation. Stirring peanut butter into cooked porridge off the heat, rather than cooking it in, preserves its flavour and gives a better texture.

content.text: Peanut butter stirred into hot porridge at the end of cooking melts into the oats and makes them deeply nutty and satisfying, more so than a spoonful on top, which sits as a separate layer and never fully combines. Banana brings sweetness and softness, and a drizzle of {{honey}} honey makes it feel finished. It is a high-protein, filling breakfast that takes the same ten minutes as plain porridge and keeps you going significantly longer.

Put the {{porridge-oats}} porridge oats in a saucepan with the {{whole-milk}} whole milk and a pinch of {{sea-salt-flakes}} sea salt flakes. Stir together and set over a medium heat. Bring slowly to a gentle simmer, stirring regularly. Once the milk is bubbling, reduce to low and cook for five to six minutes, stirring often, until the oats have absorbed the milk and the porridge is thick and creamy. The porridge should pull away from the sides of the pan when stirred and leave a clear trail.

Take the pan off the heat and stir in the {{peanut-butter}} peanut butter immediately. The residual heat of the cooked porridge is enough to melt it through without cooking it, you get the full flavour of the peanut butter rather than a roasted, slightly bitter note from heat. Stir vigorously for about thirty seconds until the peanut butter is fully incorporated and the porridge has turned a pale caramel colour. If the porridge has thickened too much, add a splash of hot milk and stir it in.

Smooth peanut butter incorporates more evenly and gives a uniform, creamy texture throughout the bowl. Crunchy adds pieces of peanut that give texture variation, particularly good against the soft oats. Use whichever you prefer, but choose a peanut butter with no added sugar or palm oil if you can: the flavour is cleaner and the oil content is more consistent, which means it stirs in more smoothly.

Spoon into warm bowls. Slice the {{banana}} banana and arrange it over the top. Drizzle over the honey if using. A pinch of extra sea salt flakes over the top is worth considering, salt amplifies both the peanut and the banana flavour considerably, and the sweet-salt contrast is the thing that makes this version of porridge taste like more than the sum of its parts. Eat immediately while the peanut butter is still warm and running through the oats.

Peanut butter porridge takes well to a few simple additions. A small spoonful of cocoa powder stirred in with the peanut butter gives a chocolate-peanut combination that tastes more indulgent than it is. A handful of granola scattered over the top adds crunch. For a dairy-free version, oat milk or a 50/50 mix of oat milk and water works well, the oat milk has enough body to give a creamy result without the richness of whole milk.

Peanut butter is not combining and sits in clumps: the porridge has cooled too much, or the peanut butter was very thick and cold from the fridge. Take the peanut butter out of the fridge at the start of cooking so it is at room temperature, and stir firmly for a full minute off the heat.
Porridge is too thick after adding peanut butter: peanut butter absorbs moisture and thickens the porridge further. Add a splash of warm milk and stir to loosen before serving.
Banana is browning before serving: slice it just before putting in the bowl, not while the porridge cooks. A squeeze of lemon juice slows browning if you need to slice ahead.
